items.stem: What is an exothermic reaction?
options: a reaction that needs a catalyst
a reaction that only happens when heated
a reaction that takes in thermal energy from the surroundings
a reaction that transfers thermal energy to the surroundings
items.answer: a reaction that transfers thermal energy to the surroundings
items.markingKey: Exothermic: energy released; surroundings get hotter.

items.stem: Explain why the temperature of the mixture falls when ammonium nitrate dissolves in water.
items.answer: The process is endothermic: thermal energy is taken in from the water (surroundings), so the temperature falls.

items.stem: Explain why a polystyrene cup with a lid is used when measuring temperature changes of reactions in solution.
items.answer: Polystyrene is an insulator and the lid reduces heat loss/gain to the surroundings, so the measured temperature change is more accurate.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: insulation; 1 mark: reduces energy transfer → more accurate [2]

items.stem: Results: experiment 1: calcium carbonate is heated strongly and decomposes; start 18 °C, end 6 °C; experiment 2: iron powder in a hand warmer reacts with oxygen; start 17 °C, end 43 °C; experiment 3: sodium hydroxide solution is added to dilute hydrochloric acid; start 19 °C, end 43 °C. Calculate the temperature change in each experiment, classify each reaction as exothermic or endothermic, and identify the experiment with the largest energy change.
items.answer: 1: −12 °C, endothermic; 2: +26 °C, exothermic; 3: +24 °C, exothermic; largest change: experiment 2
items.markingKey: 1: −12 °C, endothermic; 2: +26 °C, exothermic; 3: +24 °C, exothermic; largest change: experiment 2. 1 mark per experiment (change and classification) [3]; largest [1]

items.stem: Results: experiment 1: water is electrolysed into hydrogen and oxygen; start 19 °C, end 10 °C; experiment 2: hydrated copper(II) sulfate is heated and turns white; start 24 °C, end 12 °C; experiment 3: calcium carbonate is heated strongly and decomposes; start 22 °C, end 10 °C; experiment 4: citric acid is mixed with sodium hydrogencarbonate solution; start 19 °C, end 15 °C. Calculate the temperature change in each experiment, classify each reaction as exothermic or endothermic, and identify the experiment with the largest energy change.
items.answer: 1: −9 °C, endothermic; 2: −12 °C, endothermic; 3: −12 °C, endothermic; 4: −4 °C, endothermic; largest change: experiment 2
items.markingKey: 1: −9 °C, endothermic; 2: −12 °C, endothermic; 3: −12 °C, endothermic; 4: −4 °C, endothermic; largest change: experiment 2. 1 mark per experiment (change and classification) [4]; largest [1]

items.stem: Yusuf investigates two reactions in polystyrene cups. Reaction A: methane burns in a Bunsen burner; the temperature changes from 19 °C to 29 °C. Reaction B: ammonium chloride dissolves in water; the temperature changes from 19 °C to 15 °C. (a) State the sign of ΔH for each reaction. (b) Suggest a practical use for reaction A and for reaction B. (c) Explain why the final temperature of reaction A eventually returns to room temperature.
items.answer: (a) A negative; B positive (b) A: hand warmer / self-heating can; B: cold pack (c) once the reaction stops, heat is lost to the surroundings

items.stem: Which observation shows that a reaction in a test tube is endothermic?
items.answer: The test tube feels cold.
items.markingKey: Energy is taken in from the surroundings.

items.stem: Explain why the temperature change measured in a simple experiment is usually smaller than the true value for an exothermic reaction.
items.answer: Some heat is lost to the surroundings (air, container, thermometer) instead of raising the temperature of the solution.

items.stem: A student says, "Endothermic reactions make things cold, so they release cold." Explain the error.
items.answer: Endothermic reactions take in thermal energy from the surroundings; the surroundings lose energy and their temperature falls. "Cold" is not released.

items.stem: Explain why cold packs used for sports injuries contain substances that dissolve endothermically.
items.answer: When the substance dissolves it takes in thermal energy from the surroundings (the injury), cooling it.

items.stem: When calcium oxide is added to water, the temperature of the mixture rises. Explain this observation in terms of energy transfer and state the sign of ΔH.
items.answer: The reaction is exothermic: thermal energy is transferred to the surroundings, so their temperature rises. ΔH is negative.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: classification; 1 mark: direction of energy transfer; 1 mark: sign of ΔH [3]

items.stem: Results: experiment 1: ethanol burns in a spirit burner; start 17 °C, end 38 °C; experiment 2: photosynthesis takes place in a leaf; start 24 °C, end 15 °C; experiment 3: sodium hydroxide solution is added to dilute hydrochloric acid; start 20 °C, end 49 °C. Calculate the temperature change in each experiment, classify each reaction as exothermic or endothermic, and identify the experiment with the largest energy change.
items.answer: 1: +21 °C, exothermic; 2: −9 °C, endothermic; 3: +29 °C, exothermic; largest change: experiment 3
items.markingKey: 1: +21 °C, exothermic; 2: −9 °C, endothermic; 3: +29 °C, exothermic; largest change: experiment 3. 1 mark per experiment (change and classification) [3]; largest [1]

items.stem: Results: experiment 1: magnesium ribbon is added to dilute hydrochloric acid; start 18 °C, end 25 °C; experiment 2: ammonium chloride dissolves in water; start 24 °C, end 12 °C; experiment 3: water is electrolysed into hydrogen and oxygen; start 23 °C, end 11 °C; experiment 4: methane burns in a Bunsen burner; start 18 °C, end 38 °C. Calculate the temperature change in each experiment, classify each reaction as exothermic or endothermic, and identify the experiment with the largest energy change.
items.answer: 1: +7 °C, exothermic; 2: −12 °C, endothermic; 3: −12 °C, endothermic; 4: +20 °C, exothermic; largest change: experiment 4
items.markingKey: 1: +7 °C, exothermic; 2: −12 °C, endothermic; 3: −12 °C, endothermic; 4: +20 °C, exothermic; largest change: experiment 4. 1 mark per experiment (change and classification) [4]; largest [1]

items.stem: Priya adds hydrochloric acid in 5 cm³ portions to 25.0 cm³ of 0.500 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide in a polystyrene cup and records the temperature: 0 cm³: 22.0 °C, 5 cm³: 23.8 °C, 10 cm³: 25.6 °C, 15 cm³: 27.4 °C, 20 cm³: 29.2 °C, 25 cm³: 31.0 °C, 30 cm³: 30.5 °C, 35 cm³: 29.9 °C, 40 cm³: 29.4 °C. Describe and explain the shape of the results. State the volume of acid needed to neutralise the alkali and use it to calculate the concentration of the acid.
items.answer: Temperature rises (exothermic neutralisation) until 25.0 cm³, then falls as excess cold acid is added and heat is lost. Neutralisation at 25.0 cm³; acid concentration = 0.500 mol/dm³.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: rise – exothermic neutralisation; 1 mark: fall after end-point – no more reaction, cooler acid added; 1 mark: 25.0 cm³; 1 mark: n(alkali) = 0.0125 mol; c = 0.0125 ÷ 0.0250 = 0.500 mol/dm³ [4]

items.stem: Noah investigates two reactions in polystyrene cups. Reaction A: zinc powder is added to copper(II) sulfate solution; the temperature changes from 21 °C to 29 °C. Reaction B: potassium chloride dissolves in water; the temperature changes from 21 °C to 13 °C. (a) Calculate the temperature change for each reaction. (b) State the sign of ΔH for each reaction. (c) Explain why a polystyrene cup is used rather than a glass beaker.
items.answer: (a) A: +8 °C; B: −8 °C (b) A negative; B positive (c) polystyrene is a better insulator, reducing heat transfer with the surroundings

items.stem: Isla investigates two reactions in polystyrene cups. Reaction A: potassium hydroxide solution is added to dilute nitric acid; the temperature changes from 20 °C to 37 °C. Reaction B: photosynthesis takes place in a leaf; the temperature changes from 20 °C to 17 °C. (a) Calculate the temperature change for each reaction. (b) Classify each reaction as exothermic or endothermic, giving a reason. (c) Suggest two ways to make the results more accurate.
items.answer: (a) A: +17 °C; B: −3 °C (b) A exothermic (temperature rises); B endothermic (temperature falls) (c) use a lid; stir; use a more precise thermometer / data logger; repeat and average
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark each [2] (c) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: What is activation energy, Ea?
options: the minimum energy that colliding particles must have to react
the energy released by a reaction
the total energy of the products
items.answer: the minimum energy that colliding particles must have to react
items.markingKey: Ea: minimum energy needed for a successful collision.

items.stem: Explain why a reaction with a negative ΔH can still need heating to start it.
items.answer: The particles still need enough energy to overcome the activation energy before bonds break; once started, the energy released keeps the reaction going.

items.stem: Describe how a reaction pathway diagram for an endothermic reaction differs from one for an exothermic reaction.
items.answer: Endothermic: products are higher in energy than reactants (ΔH positive); exothermic: products lower (ΔH negative). Both show a hump for activation energy.

items.stem: On a reaction pathway diagram for the reaction of zinc with copper(II) sulfate, the reactants are at 270 kJ/mol, the products at 90 kJ/mol and the top of the energy hump at 455 kJ/mol. Calculate the enthalpy change, ΔH, and the activation energy, Ea, and state whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
items.answer: ΔH = −180 kJ/mol; Ea = 185 kJ/mol; exothermic

items.stem: On a reaction pathway diagram for the reaction of nitrogen with oxygen, the reactants are at 350 kJ/mol, the products at 135 kJ/mol and the top of the energy hump at 430 kJ/mol. Calculate the enthalpy change, ΔH, and the activation energy, Ea, and state whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
items.answer: ΔH = −215 kJ/mol; Ea = 80 kJ/mol; exothermic

items.stem: Sipho studies the combustion of methane. The reactants have an energy of 80 kJ/mol, the products 245 kJ/mol and the transition state (top of the hump) 515 kJ/mol. (a) Calculate ΔH for the reaction. (b) Calculate the activation energy. (c) Explain why the catalyst increases the rate of reaction.
items.answer: (a) +165 kJ/mol (b) 435 kJ/mol (c) lower Ea, so a greater proportion of colliding particles have energy ≥ Ea; more successful collisions per second

items.stem: On a reaction pathway diagram for an exothermic reaction, where are the products?
options: at the top of the curve
at the same level as the reactants
items.answer: below the reactants
items.markingKey: Energy is released, so products have less energy.

items.stem: What is the effect of a catalyst on a reaction pathway diagram?
options: It lowers the peak (activation energy) but does not change ΔH.
It raises the energy of the reactants.
It lowers the energy of the products.
items.answer: It lowers the peak (activation energy) but does not change ΔH.

items.stem: Explain how a catalyst increases the rate of a reaction, using a reaction pathway diagram.
items.answer: It provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy (lower peak), so a greater proportion of collisions have enough energy to react.

items.stem: A student says that a catalyst makes a reaction more exothermic. Explain the error.
items.answer: A catalyst lowers the activation energy only; the energies of the reactants and products, and so ΔH, are unchanged.

items.stem: The hydration of ethene has ΔH = +270 kJ/mol and an activation energy of 310 kJ/mol. Describe the reaction pathway diagram for this reaction, labelling ΔH and Ea, and explain what the diagram shows about the energy change.
items.answer: Products drawn above reactants; a hump between them; Ea arrow from reactants up to the peak (310 kJ/mol); ΔH arrow from reactants to products (270 kJ/mol up). The reaction is endothermic: energy is taken in from the surroundings.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: products correctly placed; 1 mark: Ea shown from reactants to peak; 1 mark: ΔH shown between reactants and products; 1 mark: exo/endo explanation [4]

items.stem: On a reaction pathway diagram for reaction X, the reactants are at 190 kJ/mol, the products at 240 kJ/mol and the top of the energy hump at 405 kJ/mol. Calculate the enthalpy change, ΔH, and the activation energy, Ea, and state whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
items.answer: ΔH = +50 kJ/mol; Ea = 215 kJ/mol; endothermic

items.stem: On a reaction pathway diagram for the hydration of ethene, the reactants are at 220 kJ/mol, the products at 20 kJ/mol and the top of the energy hump at 310 kJ/mol. Calculate the enthalpy change, ΔH, and the activation energy, Ea, and state whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
items.answer: ΔH = −200 kJ/mol; Ea = 90 kJ/mol; exothermic

items.stem: On a reaction pathway diagram for the oxidation of sulfur dioxide, the reactants are at 170 kJ/mol, the products at 375 kJ/mol and the top of the energy hump at 460 kJ/mol. Calculate the enthalpy change, ΔH, and the activation energy, Ea, and state whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
items.answer: ΔH = +205 kJ/mol; Ea = 290 kJ/mol; endothermic

items.stem: Elena studies the reaction of nitrogen with oxygen. The reactants have an energy of 60 kJ/mol, the products 310 kJ/mol and the transition state (top of the hump) 420 kJ/mol. (a) A catalyst reduces the activation energy by 220 kJ/mol. Describe the change to the diagram. (b) Explain why the catalyst increases the rate of reaction.
items.answer: (a) peak lower by 220 kJ/mol (at 200 kJ/mol); reactant and product levels unchanged (b) lower Ea, so a greater proportion of colliding particles have energy ≥ Ea; more successful collisions per second

items.stem: Omar studies the oxidation of sulfur dioxide. The reactants have an energy of 340 kJ/mol, the products 515 kJ/mol and the transition state (top of the hump) 810 kJ/mol. (a) Calculate ΔH for the reaction. (b) A catalyst reduces the activation energy by 300 kJ/mol. Describe the change to the diagram. (c) Explain why the catalyst increases the rate of reaction.
items.answer: (a) +175 kJ/mol (b) peak lower by 300 kJ/mol (at 510 kJ/mol); reactant and product levels unchanged (c) lower Ea, so a greater proportion of colliding particles have energy ≥ Ea; more successful collisions per second

items.stem: Which statement about bond breaking and bond making is correct?
options: Bond breaking is exothermic and bond making is endothermic.
Bond breaking is endothermic and bond making is exothermic.
items.answer: Bond breaking is endothermic and bond making is exothermic.
items.markingKey: Energy is needed to break bonds and released when bonds form.

items.stem: Explain, in terms of bonds, why the combustion of methane is exothermic.
items.answer: The energy released when the C=O and O–H bonds in CO₂ and H₂O are made is greater than the energy needed to break the C–H and O=O bonds.

items.stem: Explain why bond breaking is endothermic.
items.answer: Energy must be supplied to overcome the attraction between the shared electrons and the nuclei that holds the atoms together.

items.stem: Lina uses these bond energies, in kJ/mol: F–F 158, H–F 565, H–H 435. Calculate ΔH for the reaction H₂ + F₂ → 2HF.
items.answer: −537 kJ/mol

items.stem: The reaction H₂ + Br₂ → 2HBr takes place in the gas phase. Bond energies in kJ/mol: Br–Br 193, H–Br 366, H–H 436. Calculate the energy change of the reaction.
items.answer: −103 kJ/mol

items.stem: Isla uses these bond energies, in kJ/mol: Cl–Cl 242, H–Cl 431, H–H 435. Calculate ΔH for the reaction H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl. State whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic and explain your answer in terms of bond breaking and bond making.
items.answer: −185 kJ/mol (exothermic)
items.markingKey: bonds broken: 435 + 242 = 677 kJ [1]; bonds made: 2 × 431 = 862 kJ [1]; ΔH = 677 − 862 = −185 kJ/mol [1]; exothermic: more energy released making bonds than taken in breaking [1]

items.stem: Elena uses bond energies to study the reaction 2C₂H₆ + 7O₂ → 4CO₂ + 6H₂O. Bond energies (kJ/mol): C=O 805, C–C 347, C–H 413, O=O 498, O–H 464. (a) Calculate the energy needed to break the bonds in the reactants. (b) Calculate ΔH for the reaction. (c) Describe the reaction pathway diagram for this reaction.
items.answer: (a) 9136 kJ (b) −2872 kJ/mol (c) products below reactants by 2872 kJ/mol with an activation energy hump

items.stem: Arjun uses bond energies to study the reaction H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl. Bond energies (kJ/mol): Cl–Cl 242, H–Cl 431, H–H 436. (a) Calculate the energy needed to break the bonds in the reactants. (b) Calculate the energy released when the bonds in the products are made. (c) Describe the reaction pathway diagram for this reaction. (d) Suggest why the experimental value of ΔH may differ from your answer.
items.answer: (a) 678 kJ (b) 862 kJ (c) products below reactants by 184 kJ/mol with an activation energy hump (d) bond energies are averages; not all substances in gas state; heat losses in experiments

items.stem: A reaction is exothermic. What does this show about the bonds?
options: More energy is released making new bonds than is taken in breaking bonds.
The bonds in the products are weaker.
More energy is taken in breaking bonds than is released making bonds.
items.answer: More energy is released making new bonds than is taken in breaking bonds.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A reaction is exothermic. What does this show about the bonds? (b) State the equation used to calculate ΔH from bond energies.
items.answer: (a) More energy is released making new bonds than is taken in breaking bonds. (b) ΔH = total energy of bonds broken − total energy of bonds made

items.stem: Explain why ΔH values calculated from bond energies often differ from values measured by experiment.
items.answer: Bond energies are average values from many compounds; the actual bond strength depends on the molecule, and measurements may involve substances not in the gas state.

items.stem: A student calculates ΔH as (bonds made − bonds broken). Explain why this gives the wrong sign.
items.answer: ΔH = energy taken in (bonds broken) − energy given out (bonds made); reversing the subtraction reverses the sign.

items.stem: For the reaction 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, list the bonds broken and the bonds made, and explain how these determine whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
items.answer: Broken: 2 × H–H, 1 × O=O. Made: 4 × O–H. If more energy is released making bonds than is taken in breaking them, the reaction is exothermic; otherwise endothermic.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: bonds broken; 1 mark: bonds made; 1 mark: comparison rule [3]

items.stem: For the reaction C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH, list the bonds broken and the bonds made, and explain how these determine whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
items.answer: Broken: 1 × C=C, 4 × C–H, 2 × O–H. Made: 1 × C–C, 5 × C–H, 1 × C–O, 1 × O–H. If more energy is released making bonds than is taken in breaking them, the reaction is exothermic; otherwise endothermic.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: bonds broken; 1 mark: bonds made; 1 mark: comparison rule [3]

items.stem: Tomás uses these bond energies, in kJ/mol: C=C 612, C=O 805, C–H 413, O=O 498, O–H 464. Calculate ΔH for the reaction C₂H₄ + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 2H₂O.
items.answer: −1318 kJ/mol

items.stem: The reaction CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O takes place in the gas phase. Bond energies in kJ/mol: C=O 805, C–H 410, O=O 497, O–H 460. Calculate the energy change of the reaction.
items.answer: −816 kJ/mol

items.stem: Felix uses these bond energies, in kJ/mol: H–H 436, O=O 496, O–H 463. Calculate ΔH for the reaction 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.

items.stem: Use the bond energies (kJ/mol) C=O 743, C–C 348, C–H 412, O=O 496, O–H 463 to calculate the enthalpy change for the reaction C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O.
items.answer: −1690 kJ/mol

items.stem: For the reaction H₂ + I₂ → 2HI, ΔH = −12 kJ/mol. Using the bond energies (kJ/mol) H–H 435, I–I 151, calculate the bond energy of the H–I bond.
items.answer: 299 kJ/mol

items.stem: For the reaction N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, ΔH = −76 kJ/mol. Using the bond energies (kJ/mol) H–H 436, N–H 388, calculate the bond energy of the N≡N bond.
items.answer: 944 kJ/mol

items.stem: Engineers in Auckland assess the energy change of the reaction H₂ + I₂ → 2HI. Bond energies (kJ/mol): H–H 436, H–I 298, I–I 151. (a) State whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic and explain why. (b) Describe the reaction pathway diagram for this reaction.
items.answer: (a) exothermic: more energy released forming bonds than needed to break bonds (b) products below reactants by 9 kJ/mol with an activation energy hump

items.stem: Ines uses bond energies to study the reaction 2C₂H₆ + 7O₂ → 4CO₂ + 6H₂O. Bond energies (kJ/mol): C=O 805, C–C 347, C–H 413, O=O 498, O–H 464. (a) Calculate the energy needed to break the bonds in the reactants. (b) Calculate the energy released when the bonds in the products are made. (c) Calculate ΔH for the reaction. (d) Suggest why the experimental value of ΔH may differ from your answer.
items.answer: (a) 9136 kJ (b) 12008 kJ (c) −2872 kJ/mol (d) bond energies are averages; not all substances in gas state; heat losses in experiments

items.stem: Engineers in Mumbai assess the energy change of the reaction H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl. Bond energies (kJ/mol): Cl–Cl 242, H–Cl 431, H–H 435. (a) State whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic and explain why. (b) Describe the reaction pathway diagram for this reaction. items.answer: (a) exothermic: more energy released forming bonds than needed to break bonds (b) products below reactants by 185 kJ/mol with an activation energy hump (c) bond energies are averages; not all substances in gas state; heat losses in experiments

items.answer: thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate

items.stem: Omar investigates two reactions in polystyrene cups. Reaction A: magnesium ribbon is added to dilute hydrochloric acid; the temperature changes from 21 °C to 42 °C. items.answer: (a) polystyrene is a better insulator, reducing heat transfer with the surroundings (b) A: hand warmer / self-heating can; B: cold pack (c) once the reaction stops, heat is lost to the surroundings

items.stem: What does ΔH represent on a reaction pathway diagram?
options: the difference in energy between products and reactants
the height of the peak above the reactants
the energy of the products only
the height of the peak above the products
items.answer: the difference in energy between products and reactants
items.markingKey: ΔH = energy of products − energy of reactants.

items.stem: The reaction of hydrogen with chlorine has ΔH = −175 kJ/mol and an activation energy of 120 kJ/mol. Describe the reaction pathway diagram for this reaction, labelling ΔH and Ea, and explain what the diagram shows about the energy change.
items.answer: Products drawn below reactants; a hump between them; Ea arrow from reactants up to the peak (120 kJ/mol); ΔH arrow from reactants to products (175 kJ/mol down). The reaction is exothermic: energy is released to the surroundings.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: products correctly placed; 1 mark: Ea shown from reactants to peak; 1 mark: ΔH shown between reactants and products; total [3]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Describe how a reaction pathway diagram for an endothermic reaction differs from one for an exothermic reaction. (b) A student says that a catalyst makes a reaction more exothermic. Explain the error.
items.answer: (a) Endothermic: products are higher in energy than reactants (ΔH positive); exothermic: products lower (ΔH negative). Both show a hump for activation energy. (b) A catalyst lowers the activation energy only; the energies of the reactants and products, and so ΔH, are unchanged.

items.stem: On a reaction pathway diagram for the thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate, the reactants are at 220 kJ/mol, the products at 490 kJ/mol and the top of the energy hump at 715 kJ/mol. Calculate the enthalpy change, ΔH, and the activation energy, Ea, and state whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
items.answer: ΔH = +270 kJ/mol; Ea = 495 kJ/mol; endothermic

items.answer: ΔH = −150 kJ/mol; Ea = 230 kJ/mol; exothermic

items.stem: Ana studies the oxidation of sulfur dioxide. The reactants have an energy of 160 kJ/mol, the products 245 kJ/mol and the transition state (top of the hump) 315 kJ/mol. (a) Calculate ΔH for the reaction. (b) A catalyst reduces the activation energy by 70 kJ/mol. Describe the change to the diagram. (c) Explain why the catalyst increases the rate of reaction.
items.answer: (a) +85 kJ/mol (b) peak lower by 70 kJ/mol (at 245 kJ/mol); reactant and product levels unchanged (c) lower Ea, so a greater proportion of colliding particles have energy ≥ Ea; more successful collisions per second

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) What is the unit of bond energy? (b) State what is meant by bond energy.
items.answer: (a) kJ/mol (b) the energy needed to break one mole of a particular covalent bond (in the gas state)
items.markingKey: (a) Bond energy: energy to break one mole of bonds. (b) [1]

items.stem: For the reaction H₂ + F₂ → 2HF, list the bonds broken and the bonds made, and explain how these determine whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
items.answer: Broken: 1 × H–H, 1 × F–F. Made: 2 × H–F. If more energy is released making bonds than is taken in breaking them, the reaction is exothermic; otherwise endothermic.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: bonds broken; 1 mark: bonds made; 1 mark: comparison rule [3]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why ΔH values calculated from bond energies often differ from values measured by experiment. (b) Explain, in terms of bonds, why the combustion of methane is exothermic.
items.answer: (a) Bond energies are average values from many compounds; the actual bond strength depends on the molecule, and measurements may involve substances not in the gas state. (b) The energy released when the C=O and O–H bonds in CO₂ and H₂O are made is greater than the energy needed to break the C–H and O=O bonds.

items.stem: The reaction 2HCl → H₂ + Cl₂ takes place in the gas phase. Bond energies in kJ/mol: Cl–Cl 242, H–Cl 431, H–H 436. Calculate the energy change of the reaction.
items.answer: +184 kJ/mol

items.stem: Kenji uses these bond energies, in kJ/mol: Br–Br 192, C=C 614, C–Br 285, C–C 346, C–H 410. Calculate ΔH for the reaction C₂H₄ + Br₂ → C₂H₄Br₂.
items.answer: −110 kJ/mol

items.stem: Use the bond energies (kJ/mol) H–H 435, N–H 390, N≡N 941 to calculate the enthalpy change for the reaction 2NH₃ → N₂ + 3H₂.
items.answer: +94 kJ/mol

items.stem: Elena uses bond energies to study the reaction H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl. Bond energies (kJ/mol): Cl–Cl 242, H–Cl 431, H–H 436. (a) Calculate the energy needed to break the bonds in the reactants. (b) Calculate ΔH for the reaction. (c) State whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic and explain why.
items.answer: (a) 678 kJ (b) −184 kJ/mol (c) exothermic: more energy released forming bonds than needed to break bonds

items.stem: Engineers in Seoul assess the energy change of the reaction C₂H₆ + Cl₂ → C₂H₅Cl + HCl. Bond energies (kJ/mol): Cl–Cl 242, C–C 347, C–Cl 346, C–H 413, H–Cl 431. (a) Calculate the energy needed to break the bonds in the reactants. (b) State whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic and explain why. (c) Describe the reaction pathway diagram for this reaction. (d) Suggest why the experimental value of ΔH may differ from your answer.
items.answer: (a) 3067 kJ (b) exothermic: more energy released forming bonds than needed to break bonds (c) products below reactants by 122 kJ/mol with an activation energy hump (d) bond energies are averages; not all substances in gas state; heat losses in experiments

items.stem: Which type of reaction is used in self-heating cans of food?
items.answer: exothermic
items.markingKey: Heat is released to warm the food.

items.stem: When water is electrolysed into hydrogen and oxygen, the temperature of the mixture falls. Explain this observation in terms of energy transfer and state the sign of ΔH.
items.answer: The reaction is endothermic: thermal energy is taken in from the surroundings, so their temperature falls. ΔH is positive.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: classification; 1 mark: direction of energy transfer; total [2]

items.stem: When ammonium chloride dissolves in water, the temperature of the mixture falls. Explain this observation in terms of energy transfer and state the sign of ΔH.
items.answer: The reaction is endothermic: thermal energy is taken in from the surroundings, so their temperature falls. ΔH is positive.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: classification; 1 mark: direction of energy transfer; 1 mark: sign of ΔH [3]

items.stem: Results: experiment 1: water is electrolysed into hydrogen and oxygen; start 17 °C, end 14 °C; experiment 2: sodium reacts with water; start 17 °C, end 21 °C; experiment 3: potassium hydroxide solution is added to dilute nitric acid; start 19 °C, end 33 °C. Calculate the temperature change in each experiment, classify each reaction as exothermic or endothermic, and identify the experiment with the largest energy change.
items.answer: 1: −3 °C, endothermic; 2: +4 °C, exothermic; 3: +14 °C, exothermic; largest change: experiment 3
items.markingKey: 1: −3 °C, endothermic; 2: +4 °C, exothermic; 3: +14 °C, exothermic; largest change: experiment 3. 1 mark per experiment (change and classification) [3]; largest [1]

items.stem: Results: experiment 1: ethanoic acid reacts with sodium hydrogencarbonate; start 21 °C, end 9 °C; experiment 2: water is electrolysed into hydrogen and oxygen; start 21 °C, end 9 °C; experiment 3: photosynthesis takes place in a leaf; start 20 °C, end 8 °C; experiment 4: zinc powder is added to copper(II) sulfate solution; start 19 °C, end 48 °C. Calculate the temperature change in each experiment, classify each reaction as exothermic or endothermic, and identify the experiment with the largest energy change.
items.answer: 1: −12 °C, endothermic; 2: −12 °C, endothermic; 3: −12 °C, endothermic; 4: +29 °C, exothermic; largest change: experiment 4
items.markingKey: 1: −12 °C, endothermic; 2: −12 °C, endothermic; 3: −12 °C, endothermic; 4: +29 °C, exothermic; largest change: experiment 4. 1 mark per experiment (change and classification) [4]; largest [1]

items.stem: Sipho investigates two reactions in polystyrene cups. Reaction A: calcium oxide is added to water; the temperature changes from 19 °C to 27 °C. Reaction B: citric acid is mixed with sodium hydrogencarbonate solution; the temperature changes from 19 °C to 12 °C. (a) Explain why a polystyrene cup is used rather than a glass beaker. (b) Suggest two ways to make the results more accurate. (c) Explain why the final temperature of reaction A eventually returns to room temperature.
items.answer: (a) polystyrene is a better insulator, reducing heat transfer with the surroundings (b) use a lid; stir; use a more precise thermometer / data logger; repeat and average (c) once the reaction stops, heat is lost to the surroundings

items.stem: State the meaning of the symbol ΔH.
items.answer: enthalpy change (energy transferred) of a reaction

items.stem: The reaction of hydrogen with chlorine has ΔH = +245 kJ/mol and an activation energy of 430 kJ/mol. Describe the reaction pathway diagram for this reaction, labelling ΔH and Ea, and explain what the diagram shows about the energy change.
items.answer: Products drawn above reactants; a hump between them; Ea arrow from reactants up to the peak (430 kJ/mol); ΔH arrow from reactants to products (245 kJ/mol up). The reaction is endothermic: energy is taken in from the surroundings.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: products correctly placed; 1 mark: Ea shown from reactants to peak; 1 mark: ΔH shown between reactants and products; total [3]

items.stem: Reaction X has ΔH = +230 kJ/mol and an activation energy of 290 kJ/mol. Describe the reaction pathway diagram for this reaction, labelling ΔH and Ea, and explain what the diagram shows about the energy change.
items.answer: Products drawn above reactants; a hump between them; Ea arrow from reactants up to the peak (290 kJ/mol); ΔH arrow from reactants to products (230 kJ/mol up). The reaction is endothermic: energy is taken in from the surroundings.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: products correctly placed; 1 mark: Ea shown from reactants to peak; 1 mark: ΔH shown between reactants and products; 1 mark: exo/endo explanation [4]

items.stem: On a reaction pathway diagram for the oxidation of sulfur dioxide, the reactants are at 100 kJ/mol, the products at 390 kJ/mol and the top of the energy hump at 585 kJ/mol. Calculate the enthalpy change, ΔH, and the activation energy, Ea, and state whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
items.answer: ΔH = +290 kJ/mol; Ea = 485 kJ/mol; endothermic

items.stem: On a reaction pathway diagram for the oxidation of sulfur dioxide, the reactants are at 160 kJ/mol, the products at 450 kJ/mol and the top of the energy hump at 600 kJ/mol. Calculate the enthalpy change, ΔH, and the activation energy, Ea, and state whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
items.answer: ΔH = +290 kJ/mol; Ea = 440 kJ/mol; endothermic

items.stem: Felix studies the formation of ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen. The reactants have an energy of 100 kJ/mol, the products 45 kJ/mol and the transition state (top of the hump) 360 kJ/mol. (a) Calculate the activation energy. (b) State and explain whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic. (c) Explain why the catalyst increases the rate of reaction.
items.answer: (a) 260 kJ/mol (b) exothermic: products lower than reactants, energy released (c) lower Ea, so a greater proportion of colliding particles have energy ≥ Ea; more successful collisions per second

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) State the equation used to calculate ΔH from bond energies. (b) A reaction is exothermic. What does this show about the bonds?
items.answer: (a) ΔH = total energy of bonds broken − total energy of bonds made (b) More energy is released making new bonds than is taken in breaking bonds.

items.stem: For the reaction H₂ + Br₂ → 2HBr, list the bonds broken and the bonds made, and explain how these determine whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
items.answer: Broken: 1 × H–H, 1 × Br–Br. Made: 2 × H–Br. If more energy is released making bonds than is taken in breaking them, the reaction is exothermic; otherwise endothermic.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: bonds broken; 1 mark: bonds made; 1 mark: comparison rule [3]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why ΔH values calculated from bond energies often differ from values measured by experiment. (b) A student calculates ΔH as (bonds made − bonds broken). Explain why this gives the wrong sign.
items.answer: (a) Bond energies are average values from many compounds; the actual bond strength depends on the molecule, and measurements may involve substances not in the gas state. (b) ΔH = energy taken in (bonds broken) − energy given out (bonds made); reversing the subtraction reverses the sign.

items.stem: Ethan uses these bond energies, in kJ/mol: H–H 436, H–I 299, I–I 151. Calculate ΔH for the reaction 2HI → H₂ + I₂.
items.answer: +11 kJ/mol
items.markingKey: bonds broken: 2 × 299 = 598 kJ [1]; bonds made: 436 + 151 = 587 kJ [1]; ΔH = 598 − 587 = +11 kJ/mol [1]
